scoreNote: Strong (5): agrees privacy is eroding, then argues the claim's cause is too narrow because corporate and government collection do most of the damage, and that a right is not the same as its exercise; addresses the claim directly.

sentences.text: We broadcast our locations, opinions, purchases, and faces to the world, then wonder why nothing feels private anymore.
The claim draws the obvious conclusion, holding that because people increasingly feel compelled to share their personal details online, the right to privacy is eroding.

The claim is right that privacy is eroding, but its explanation is too simple, for voluntary oversharing is only part of the story, and a right does not vanish merely because people choose not to exercise it.
The claim is correct about the basic fact: privacy really is in retreat.
More of our lives is recorded, shared, and stored than ever before, and information once private — where we go, what we buy, whom we know — is now routinely exposed.
Much of this we do voluntarily, posting details we would once have guarded and feeling steady social pressure to share ever more of our lives online.
A generation ago, the details now scattered across distant servers would have lived only in our own memories.
On the central observation — that privacy is shrinking — the claim is plainly right.

sections.role: Body — But the cause is broader

sentences.text: However, the claim blames the wrong culprit, or at least far too narrow a one.
Privacy is eroded less by what people willingly post than by what is taken from them without their knowledge or consent.
Corporations harvest vast data on people who share nothing willingly, and governments surveil citizens who never chose to be watched, so the deepest threats to privacy are not voluntary at all.
To pin the erosion of privacy mainly on people's compulsion to share is to excuse the powerful institutions that quietly do most of the eroding.
The most invasive watchers are precisely the ones we never knowingly agreed to.
Voluntary oversharing is real, but it is far from the main force destroying privacy.

sections.role: Body — A right is not its exercise

sentences.text: Moreover, the claim confuses the erosion of privacy in practice with the erosion of the right to it.

A right to privacy does not disappear simply because people choose to share, since one can give away one's privacy while fully retaining the right to it, just as one can waive a right without losing it.
The right erodes only when law and society stop protecting privacy, allowing it to be taken regardless of consent, which is a political failure rather than a personal one.
That people overshare is a cultural habit that could change tomorrow, whereas whether the right survives depends on whether we still defend it in law.
Privacy as a practice may be fading, but the right to it stands or falls on what we are willing to protect.
In conclusion, the claim is right that privacy is eroding, but wrong to trace it mainly to people's compulsion to share.

Privacy really is in retreat, yet the heaviest blows come from corporate and governmental collection rather than from voluntary posting, and the right to privacy survives our oversharing, eroding only if we let law and society stop defending it.
We are giving away our privacy, but we have not yet lost the right to demand it back.
